but he didn’t care. He went inside the Ohel and davened with all his might that his grandchild should be born healthy.

One month later, the baby boy was born. Many doctors were there at the birth, ready to rush him to surgery.

“Hmm … his oxygen levels are surprisingly good,” one of the doctors noted. “Let’s do an ultrasound to get a picture of his heart before we send him off.”

When they saw the picture, the doctors were shocked. The baby’s heart looked normal! The problem was completely gone!

“Let’s use a different ultrasound machine just in case,” the doctors decided. Once again, the tests came back normal.

They then brought in a top doctor, who declared that the baby was totally healthy.

The doctors couldn’t believe it. They repeated the test every day to make sure that the baby’s heart was truly fine. When the results kept coming back normal, they decided to test every week, and then every month. Finally, they gave up.

“We can’t explain it, but your baby’s heart healed miraculously on its own!” they told the overjoyed parents.

Of course, Uncle Yitzchak told his family about that rainy Lag Ba’Omer tefillah at the

A few times a year, they visit Ohel together with their miracle son, whom they named Eli Lev, to thank the Rebbe for the bracha that has changed their family b’gashmius and b’ruchnius.

Uncle Yitzchak was about to turn around and go back home. All of a sudden, the skies began to pour, clearing the way for him to get a bracha from the Rebbe.

Our great-uncle Yitzchak lives in New York and is growing in his Yiddishkeit. A few years ago, he was expecting a new grandchild. But the doctors didn’t have good news to share.

“The baby has a big heart problem,” they said. “As soon as he is born, he will need emergency heart surgery.”

Uncle Yitzchak was devastated. As he sat in his store one day thinking about the baby, two bochurim walked inside. “Did you put on tefillin today?” they asked with friendly smiles.

“I did,” Yitzchak answered. “I always make sure to put on tefillin.”

“That’s amazing!” the boys replied happily. They began to chat, and Uncle Yitzchak shared the difficult news about his soon-to-be-born grandchild.

“Do you know that today is Lag Ba’Omer?” one bochur asked.

“You should go to the Ohel of the Lubavitcher Rebbe,” the other continued. “The Rebbe says that kevarim of all tzadikim are connected.

When you daven at the Rebbe’s Ohel, it’s like davening at Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai’s kever in Meron!”

“I’ve never heard of Lag Ba’Omer,” Uncle Yitzchak said. “I’ll find out more about it.”

But the bochurim didn’t want him to wait. “Lag Ba’Omer is a special day to get brachos for children. Go to the Ohel before the day is over! We’re sure that the Rebbe’s brachos will help.”

Uncle Yitzchak was finally convinced and drove to Queens. But when he got to the Ohel, there was a very long line.

I don’t have time to wait so long, he thought. I’ll just go back home...
